description: How gender, age, race, religion, family and disability shape participation in physical activity.
content_html:
What Are Engagement Patterns?

Engagement patterns describe who participates in physical activity, how often, and in which activities. They vary significantly across different social groups — not because of differences in ability, but because of the social, cultural, economic and practical factors that shape people’s lives. Understanding why participation differs between groups is central to this topic, because the goal of sport policy and education is to remove barriers and make physical activity genuinely accessible to all.

The specification identifies five social groups whose engagement patterns merit specific study: gender, race and religion (including culture), age, family and friends (peers), and people with a disability. For each group, a range of factors can either promote or discourage participation. These factors are not mutually exclusive — a person’s engagement is typically shaped by a combination of several simultaneously.

Gender and Engagement Patterns

Despite significant progress in recent decades, engagement patterns in the UK still differ between men and women. Women and girls historically face additional barriers that reduce their participation rates in many formal and competitive sports. Sexism and stereotyping play a documented role: cultural assumptions that sport is a male domain discourage participation, particularly at secondary school age when peer opinion carries heavy social weight. Media coverage is a powerful amplifier: women’s sport receives a fraction of broadcast time compared to men’s sport in most disciplines, which limits the visibility of female role models and reduces the perceived status of women’s sport.

Role models matter enormously to engagement. When Beth Mead scored a hat-trick in England’s opening game of the 2022 UEFA Women’s Euros, junior girls’ football club registrations spiked across England. Similarly, Dame Sarah Storey’s Paralympic cycling gold medals have been credited with increasing female disability sport participation. The absence of visible female role models in a sport creates a self-reinforcing cycle: girls don’t see women competing, so they don’t believe the sport is for them. Family commitments also fall disproportionately on women across all age groups, reducing available leisure time. Socio-economic factors intersect here too: lower-income households, where women are statistically over-represented, may have less disposable income to spend on sport memberships, equipment and travel.

Key Fact

Key factors limiting female engagement: sexism and stereotyping (cultural assumptions about suitability), limited media coverage (reduces role model visibility), family commitments (reduces available leisure time), and socio-economic factors (lower disposable income, fewer facilities in lower-income areas). Positive role models such as Beth Mead and Dame Sarah Storey have demonstrably increased participation.

Race, Religion and Culture

Engagement patterns can differ significantly between ethnic and religious groups. Race-based discrimination in sport — from unconscious bias in recruitment to overt racist behaviour from crowds — creates hostile environments that deter participation. In football, cricket and athletics, governing bodies have run high-profile campaigns to address racism, acknowledging that even elite sport is not free from this barrier.

Religion and culture add further dimensions. Religious festivals, prayer times and dietary requirements can create scheduling conflicts with training and competition. A Muslim athlete observing Ramadan fasts may find the energy demands of high-intensity training during that period challenging, requiring coaches and clubs to show flexibility. Cultural norms within some communities restrict female participation in mixed-sex sport or sport where clothing requirements conflict with modesty expectations. Familiarity also matters: if a sport has no visible presence within a particular cultural community, members of that community may not encounter it, learn its rules or perceive it as accessible. Education and community outreach can address this, but change is slow.

Age

Participation patterns change across the life course. Young people tend to participate at higher rates when physical education is compulsory, activity is part of the school day and peer social groups are built around sport. After leaving school, participation often drops sharply — a phenomenon described in research as the “dropout cliff” — as competing demands of higher education, work and family life reduce available leisure time and physical activity becomes optional rather than compulsory.

Older adults face different barriers: declining physical capacity, increased risk of injury, fewer accessible facilities, and reduced social networks following retirement or bereavement. However, accessible and appropriate activities — such as walking football, seated yoga, aqua aerobics and bowls — can sustain engagement among older populations. Attitudes towards ageing also matter: negative stereotypes around older people and sport discourage participation and undermine the confidence of individuals who might otherwise be active. The role of attitudes — both the individual’s own and those of those around them — is a consistent theme across all groups.

Family is one of the strongest predictors of physical activity in children. Children whose parents participate in sport are significantly more likely to be active themselves — parents model behaviour, provide transport, pay fees, and signal through their own choices that sport is worthwhile. Conversely, family commitments can be the biggest barrier to adult female participation in particular, as childcare and caring responsibilities disproportionately reduce available leisure time for women.

Peers carry enormous influence in adolescence: young people are more likely to participate if their friendship group is active, and more likely to drop out if sport is not part of their social identity. Socio-economic factors cut across all groups: socio-economic factors such as disposable income determine whether a family can afford club memberships, specialist equipment, coaching fees and travel. Free or low-cost community sport programmes are therefore critical to equitable access, particularly for young people in lower-income households.

Disability

People with physical or intellectual disabilities historically face some of the most significant barriers to participation in sport. These fall into physical and attitudinal categories. Physical barriers include inaccessible facilities (steps rather than ramps, no accessible changing rooms, pools without hoist equipment), lack of adapted equipment, and absence of disability-specific sessions or coaching. Attitudinal barriers are often harder to address: negative stereotypes assume that people with disabilities are not interested in or capable of sport at competitive level, despite extensive evidence to the contrary. Dame Sarah Storey’s 17 Paralympic gold medals, Jonnie Peacock’s 100 m sprint title at London 2012 and the growth of wheelchair basketball as a spectator sport all challenge these assumptions.

Adaptability and inclusiveness of facilities and activities are therefore key factors. Where clubs, leisure centres and governing bodies have invested in adaptive provision — deaf-friendly coaching, wheelchair-accessible courts, sitting volleyball, boccia, goalball — participation among disabled groups has increased. The relationship between disability and engagement underlines the broader principle: removing practical barriers and challenging negative attitudes are the twin levers for improving engagement patterns across all under-represented groups.

Key Fact

Barriers for disabled people: physical (inaccessible facilities, no adapted equipment, no disability sessions) and attitudinal (stereotyping, negative assumptions about capability and interest). Adaptability and inclusiveness of provision are the key solutions. Role models like Dame Sarah Storey and Jonnie Peacock challenge stereotypes and raise visibility.

Several factors appear as barriers across multiple groups, not just one. Role models: absence of visible, relatable role models reduces aspirational engagement for any under-represented group. Media coverage: low media coverage limits the perceived legitimacy and interest of a group’s participation. Accessibility: physical access to facilities matters across gender, age, disability and socio-economic status. Attitudes: both the individual’s own attitudes and the attitudes of coaches, clubs and institutions affect whether individuals feel welcome. Education: schools and community programmes that introduce diverse young people to a wide range of activities early build habits of participation that often persist into adulthood. Recognising these cross-cutting factors helps answer exam questions that ask you to explain multiple barriers or evaluate strategies to increase engagement.
exam_tip_html: On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question about engagement patterns, you must do three things: quote a specific figure from the data, make a comparison, and explain what it means in a sporting context. Simply reading a number off a table earns nothing by itself — the mark scheme rewards the inference. For example: “School B has 27% participation compared to School A’s 18% — a difference of 9 percentage points — suggesting School B has more inclusive provision or stronger role model visibility.” On a 9 marks — Evaluate question about factors affecting engagement, a common error is listing only one group’s barriers. Full marks require multiple factors applied across different groups, with balanced points (both barriers and enabling factors), sporting examples and a justified conclusion. Use the cross-cutting factors (role models, media, socio-economic access) as a framework to structure a balanced answer.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Engagement patterns measure who participates in physical activity and why. They differ between social groups because of social, cultural, economic and practical barriers, not inherent differences in ability or interest.
  • Key groups with documented lower engagement include women (sexism, stereotyping, less media coverage, family commitments), ethnic and religious minorities (discrimination, cultural and scheduling conflicts), older adults (physical decline, stereotypes, fewer accessible activities), and people with disabilities (inaccessible facilities, attitudinal barriers).
  • Cross-cutting solutions include positive role models, improved media coverage of under-represented groups, accessible and inclusive facilities, removal of socio-economic barriers, and education that introduces a wide range of activities to young people early.

practice_questions.text: Identify one factor related to media coverage that could reduce female participation in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid response linking media coverage to reduced female participation, e.g.: women's sport receives less broadcast time than men's sport, reducing the visibility of female role models; lack of media coverage means female sport is perceived as less important or prestigious; girls are less likely to see women competing and therefore less likely to aspire to participate.

practice_questions.text: State two factors related to disability that can reduce a person's participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid factor, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: inaccessible facilities (e.g. no ramps, no hoist equipment in pools); lack of adapted equipment; absence of disability-specific coaching sessions; negative stereotyping by coaches or institutions; attitudinal barriers (assumptions that disabled people are not interested in or capable of sport); lack of role models in disability sport.

practice_questions.text: Describe how socio-economic factors can affect engagement patterns in physical activity. Give an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining or explaining what socio-economic factors are (related to income, social class, occupation — factors that affect disposable income and available leisure time); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism — lower income means less money for club memberships, equipment, transport or specialist coaching, making sport less accessible; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. a family with limited income cannot afford football club fees, sports kit or travel to away fixtures; free-to-use community sport programmes are therefore critical).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows participation in organised sport among four social groups at a secondary school over one term.

Group | Participation rate
Male students | 68%
Female students | 41%
Students with a disability | 22%
Students from lower socio-economic backgrounds | 35%

Using the data in Table 1, interpret what the data shows about engagement patterns at this school and suggest one reason for the lowest participation rate shown.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the lowest participation group (students with a disability, 22%); 1 mark for making a valid comparison using figures (e.g. students with a disability participate at 22% compared to 68% for male students — a gap of 46 percentage points); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (disabled students are significantly less likely to participate in organised sport, suggesting barriers to access or inclusion at this school); 1 mark for suggesting one valid reason for the low rate (inaccessible facilities, lack of adapted provision, attitudinal barriers from staff or peers, negative stereotyping, absence of disability sport sessions or role models).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the factors that explain why engagement patterns in physical activity differ between older adults (aged 60+) and young adults (aged 18–30).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains at least three contrasting factors across both age groups, applying each specifically to the age group. For older adults: physical decline (reduced strength, flexibility, cardiovascular endurance, increased injury risk), fewer social networks, reduced available provision, negative stereotypes about ageing and sport, reduced leisure time in pre-retirement years. For young adults: transition out of compulsory education removes structured activity, competing demands of work and family reduce leisure time, dropout cliff phenomenon as sport becomes optional. Recognises enabling factors for older adults (walking football, aqua aerobics, adapted provision). Developed prose with sporting examples.

Secure: Addresses both age groups with at least two factors per group and some explanation of mechanism. Sporting application present. May lack full balance or detailed development.

Developing: Identifies relevant factors but treats them superficially. May focus on only one age group or list without explanation. Sporting context limited.

Emerging: Basic points only. Little age-specific application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which role models are the most important factor in improving engagement patterns among under-represented groups in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with well-developed points on both sides. Arguments in support: positive role models give under-represented groups aspirational figures who look like them, demonstrating that sport is possible (e.g. Beth Mead and women's football registrations, Dame Sarah Storey and disability sport); they increase media coverage indirectly by making their sport more commercially attractive; they challenge stereotypes that deter participation. Arguments against or limitations: role models alone cannot overcome structural barriers such as inaccessible facilities, socio-economic cost, scheduling conflicts related to religion or family, or institutionalised discrimination; media coverage and accessibility are arguably more systemic levers; without affordable, accessible provision, a role model's inspiration cannot translate into actual participation. Justified conclusion reached, e.g. role models are necessary but insufficient — they must be accompanied by structural changes in access and provision. Sporting examples throughout.

Secure: Both sides with some development. At least one limitation of relying solely on role models identified. Conclusion present. Examples used.

Developing: Mostly one-sided. Some relevant points but limited development. Sporting application limited.

Emerging: Basic, largely descriptive. No meaningful balance or evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes the rates and patterns of participation in physical activity across different groups in society?
Which of the following best explains why limited media coverage of women's sport reduces female participation?
options: Women are less interested in competitive sport than men
Media coverage determines how much prize money is available
Lack of visible role models makes sport seem less accessible or aspirational to girls
Television viewing figures directly fund club memberships

knowledge_checks.q: Negative _____ about older people and sport discourage participation and undermine confidence among people who might otherwise be active.
_____ factors, such as disposable income and access to facilities, affect whether individuals can afford to participate in organised sport.
Match each social group to one specific barrier to sport participation:
right: Sexism and stereotyping limiting perceived suitability for sport
Inaccessible facilities and negative attitudes about capability
Physical decline and fewer organised activities designed for them

flashcard_questions.q: What are engagement patterns in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: The rates and patterns of participation across different social groups, revealing inequalities in access.

flashcard_questions.q: What is sexism in sport and how does it affect engagement?
flashcard_questions.a: Prejudice based on sex; reduces female participation by creating hostile environments and limiting opportunities.

flashcard_questions.q: How does limited media coverage of women's sport affect participation?
flashcard_questions.a: It reduces visible role models, making sport seem less accessible or aspirational to girls.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one way a positive role model can increase engagement patterns.
flashcard_questions.a: Visible success by someone from an under-represented group inspires others in that group to participate.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one physical barrier that reduces sport participation for people with a disability.
flashcard_questions.a: Inaccessible facilities, such as no ramps or no hoist equipment in swimming pools.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one attitudinal barrier that reduces sport participation for people with a disability.
flashcard_questions.a: Stereotyping — assumptions that disabled people are not interested in or capable of competitive sport.

flashcard_questions.q: How do socio-economic factors limit sport participation?
flashcard_questions.a: Lower income reduces ability to pay for club memberships, equipment, coaching and transport.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does participation in sport often drop after young people leave school?
flashcard_questions.a: Activity becomes optional and competing demands of work, education and family reduce leisure time.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one cultural or religious factor that can reduce sport participation.
flashcard_questions.a: Prayer times or religious festivals creating scheduling conflicts with training and competition.

flashcard_questions.q: How does family influence a child's engagement in physical activity?
flashcard_questions.a: Children whose parents participate in sport are more likely to be active — parents model behaviour and provide support.

flashcard_questions.q: What two things must adaptability and inclusiveness of provision address to improve disability engagement?
flashcard_questions.a: Physical accessibility of facilities and negative attitudinal barriers from institutions and coaches.

glossary_terms.definition: The rates and patterns of participation in physical activity across different groups in society, often used to identify inequalities in access and involvement.
Prejudice, stereotyping or discrimination based on a person's sex, which in sport often manifests as assumptions about female capability, interest or suitability for physical activity.
An oversimplified, fixed image or idea about what members of a particular group are like, often used to exclude individuals from activities assumed not to suit their group.
Factors related to social class and economic position, including income, occupation and education level, that influence access to sport facilities, equipment, coaching and leisure time.
Adapted or specific sporting activities designed to be accessible to participants with physical or learning disabilities, enabling full participation in physical activity.
Social norms, traditions or expectations within a community that discourage or prevent certain groups from participating in particular sports or physical activities.

items.title: Don't Tell Me the Score — Dame Sarah Storey: Disability Sport and Challenging Stereotypes
items.description: Simon Mundie explores how Storey's success challenged attitudinal barriers in disability sport and what her medals mean for participation by people with disabilities.

items.title: High Performance Podcast — Beth Mead on Women's Football, Visibility and Role Models
items.description: Jake Humphrey and Damian Hughes discuss how increased media coverage, role models like Mead and the Euros 2022 effect have shifted engagement patterns for women and girls in football.

items.title: What Makes a Good Life? — Robert Waldinger | TED
items.description: Harvard's longest study on human flourishing shows how social connection and community participation — including sport — shapes wellbeing across different social groups and ages.

items.title: The Happy Secret to Better Work — Shawn Achor | TED
items.description: Achor's positive psychology research on wellbeing, belonging and community connects directly to why accessible sport participation across social groups improves life outcomes.

items.title: How to Motivate Yourself to Change — Tali Sharot | TEDxCambridge
items.description: Sharot's work on behaviour change explains why removing barriers to participation — not just raising awareness — is needed to shift engagement patterns in under-represented groups.

items.title: Bend It Like Beckham (2002)
items.description: A vivid dramatisation of cultural barriers, gender stereotyping and family expectations that restrict engagement for young women from South Asian backgrounds — essential context for socio-cultural analysis.

items.title: Sunderland 'Til I Die (2018)
items.description: The Netflix series explores how socio-economic decline, community identity and class affect sport participation and engagement patterns in a post-industrial town.

items.title: Sport England — Active Lives Survey
items.description: The definitive UK dataset on sport participation rates by gender, age, disability, ethnicity and socio-economic group — real data to support exam answers on engagement patterns.

items.title: BBC Bitesize — Social Groups and Engagement Patterns in PE
items.description: AQA-aligned notes on gender, race, religion, age, disability and socio-economic factors that shape engagement in physical activity, with exam-style question practice.
